title: Medicine Hat, Alta., seeks to become 'drone city' as defence dollars roll in
summary: As Canada boosts its military spending, officials in Medicine Hat, Alta., are seeking out new investment and economic activity tied to new private sector engagement by the Canadian Forces at CFB…

image.caption: Models of unmanned aircraft sit on a display table during a conference on defence investment in southeastern Alberta on Oct. 29 in Medicine Hat. (Collin Gallant/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary

As Canada boosts its military spending, officials in Medicine Hat, Alta., are seeking out new investment and economic activity tied to new private sector engagement by the Canadian Forces at CFB Suffield.
Long known as 'Gas City,' southern Alberta community seeks new investment
It's half the size of Prince Edward Island under a wide prairie sky and could be a launch pad for economic development and diversification in southeast Alberta.

Local officials, the Canadian Forces and private defence contractors say Canadian Forces Base Suffield is a key piece to upgrade Canada's military and potentially bring high-tech drone testing, new defence spending and jobs to the region that is dominated now by ranching and oilpatch activity.

"I think that CFB Suffield is the secret weapon in the arsenal of tools that southeast Alberta has to grow in the defence industry," said Lt.-Col. Mike Onieu, a former base commander of the 2,700-square-kilometre firing range located about 50 kilometres west of Medicine Hat.

Now in charge of future projects at the base, Onieu told 220 delegates at a defence forum in Medicine Hat on Oct. 29 that his mission is to maximize the facility in light of a national strategy to boost domestic defence research and drone technology.
"Most importantly, we need to unlock the base for third-party uses," he told the audience, which included private sector defence contractors.
"We understand the incredible demand by industry and third parties to access the base. We haven't figured out how that's going to look yet, but it is going to happen."
Companies' desire to use the heavily restricted space — potentially bringing work crews and researchers, or potentially locating operations nearby — is what Medicine Hat is banking on.
City seeks new investment, new direction

Long known as the "Gas City," the city located 300 kilometres from Calgary is attempting to reinvent itself as the "Drone City" — a campaign to lure entrepreneurs, engineers and skilled high-tech trade workers from larger centres to work in the aerospace industry.

A commercial showcasing the community, its amenities, short commutes and lower housing costs debuted earlier this month during the national broadcasts of a recent curling event held at the city's 6,000-seat junior hockey arena.
Front and centre are drone companies already in the city, located to take advantage of Suffield's proximity.

"The companies that we have here now want to grow," Mayor Linnsie Clark told CBC News at the same city-sponsored defence conference. She sees the city's role in "workforce attraction" to "empower" that growth.
"[Then], naturally, some of their partners in the supply chain or [work] they're contracting out to other places now, will hopefully move to Medicine Hat.
"That is truly an integrated cluster."
Three major drone companies in the city already employ about 100 workers — notable in the city of 69,000 — but economic officials believe much more is possible.

The city, Medicine Hat College, several economic development groups and private industry are collaborating to create a "defence innovation hub." It seeks to remove barriers for high-tech firms and spur stagnant local economic and population growth.
Aerospace development is a key pillar of a four-year economic development plan of municipalities in the region.

"There's an appetite to attract new business, expand the current business," said Vincent Malley, head of business development for UVA Dynamics, a drone developer in Medicine Hat now competing for contracts in the recently announced European defence bank.
"Leveraging those assets that we have, it gives a foundation to be able to do that."

Lt.-Col. Mike Onieu is head of evaluating future projects at Canadian Forces Base Suffield, a huge military live-fire range near Medicine Hat that is now increasingly used for drone research. (Collin Gallant/CBC)
New investment in drones, research
Canada's military leaders have promised fast action to integrate drones into Canadian Forces and make procurement a faster and more efficient process for private industry.
The latest federal budget includes $2 billion over five years specific to drone capabilities as the overall defence budget grows.

blocks.text: The Defence Research and Development Canada facility at the base currently employs about 180 scientists and support workers.

The Forces operation at the base employs 220 employees, according to the Department of National Defence — about 200 less than when Canada supported annual British Army tank training exercises for up to 10,000 troops.
New drone-defence technology put to the test at Canadian showcase

The British military moved heavy armour training to Eastern Europe in 2023, but returned to Alberta this year for smaller drone-focused exercises. Two similar deployments for drone testing and anti-drone training are scheduled for 2027, said Onieu.
Canada also held a similar "Sandbox" exercise this fall — inviting contractors to test prototypes and receive feedback from military officials at an early stage of development.

Onieu said that sort of industry engagement will continue at Suffield as its size allows secure remote spaces to evaluate electronic signal-jamming technology and other anti-drone measures away from civilian populations.
Susan Rowsell, the chief scientist at Defence Research and Development Canada at Suffield, said the base's proving ground is large enough and secure enough to test military applications.
"You can't just go and do this in the soccer field or at the Medicine Hat airport," said Rowsell.
"There are certain things you just can't do outside of this area."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Collin Gallant is a journalist with the CBC's bureau in Medicine Hat, Alta., covering a wide array of topics in southeast Alberta. Reach him by email at collin.gallant@cbc.ca
